name: Muffin
subtitle: Wii U emulation on iOS, in the open.
description: The source for Muffin - a genuine port of the Cemu Wii U emulator to iOS, built from source in the open. Work in progress, and honest about it: see STATUS.md in the repository for exactly what works and what does not. This source serves the standard build for SideStore, AltStore and LiveContainer, which re-sign it with your own Apple ID at install.

apps.name: Muffin
apps.subtitle: Wii U emulator for iPhone and iPad
apps.localizedDescription:
Muffin is the Cemu Wii U emulator, ported to iOS - iPhone and iPad, iOS 15 and later. The real C++ engine - PowerPC interpreter, ARM64 recompiler, the full Cafe OS HLE stack and Cemu's native Metal renderer - running under a SwiftUI shell.

This is in-progress software. A picture reaches the screen for real titles, but it is not yet a correct one, and no title has been confirmed playable end to end. The project documents its own state honestly rather than claiming more than it delivers - read STATUS.md before installing.

This source serves the standard build for SideStore, AltStore and LiveContainer, which re-sign it with your own Apple ID at install.

Bring your own games. No copyrighted content is distributed here.

Install with SideStore/AltStore, which re-signs with your own Apple ID.
`Cemu.app.dSYM.zip` is only needed to symbolicate a crash report.

Built from `main`.

Check the `Init Cemu <sha>` line at the top of the log before judging a
build — it names the commit that is actually in the binary, and it is the
only reliable way to tell one build from another.

No behavior changed - it's the same file-picker/import flow shipped in v1.12, just a different glyph on the button. `doc.badge.plus` matches the badge-plus pattern iOS uses elsewhere for "add a new item to a local library" (Photos, Files, etc.), which is a slightly better semantic fit for adding a ROM to Muffin's game library than either arrow direction.

Everything else is unchanged from v1.12/v1.11 - still waiting on the graphics diagnostic test (`GX2SwapScanBuffers() reached for the first time` in the log, from `helloworld.rpx`) whenever you get to it.

New feature: in-app ROM upload.

Previously the only way to get a ROM onto the device was Files-app file sharing into Documents/Roms. This adds a real upload button in the library header (next to favorites/settings) that opens the system file picker directly - Files, iCloud Drive, or anywhere else a ROM might live.

- Icon: `arrow.up.doc` (a document with an upward arrow - importing a file in, not Apple's Share glyph `square.and.arrow.up`).
- Validates the picked file's extension against the same formats the library already scans for (`wua`/`wud`/`iso`/`rpx`).
- Copies it into `Documents/Roms`, releasing security-scoped access whether the copy succeeds or fails.
- Refreshes the library immediately after a successful import.
- Shows an alert if the file's unsupported or the copy fails, instead of silently doing nothing.

v1.9 fixed the recurring crash (MetalLayerHandle double-release) - confirmed on your iPad Pro 2020 test: no crash, boot completes, log reaches "Run title". But the screen stayed black.

## The bug

`CreateMetalLayer()` (MetalLayer.mm) set the on-screen `CAMetalLayer`'s frame from `view.bounds`, read synchronously the instant the render surface registers - which happens in `makeUIView`, before SwiftUI has necessarily laid the owning view out to a nonzero size. `view.bounds` was frequently still `CGRectZero` at that exact moment, producing a layer that renders correctly internally but occupies zero screen space - invisible. Nothing later re-synced the frame either, since a manually-added sublayer doesn't auto-resize with its superlayer.

## The fix

Pass the already-known pixel size straight into `CreateMetalLayer` instead of trusting `view.bounds`, so the on-screen frame is correct regardless of SwiftUI's layout timing.

## Confidence

This matches the black-screen-with-clean-logs symptom exactly, and the code path is simple enough to be confident in the diagnosis - but same as always, wants a real device test before calling it done.

2. Launch - should not crash (confirmed already in v1.9).
3. Load `helloworld.rpx` (included) and tap play.
4. This time, watch for something to actually appear on screen, not just a clean log.
5. Check `Documents/CemuCrashLog.txt` either way.

This is the fix for the real, root-cause bug behind the recurring crash - found by tracing why two prior fixes both failed at the exact same crash location.

## The actual bug

MetalLayerHandle (the class wrapping the real drawing surface) has a destructor that releases its underlying layer, but no matching move or copy behavior defined - a specific, well-known C++ rule violation. Every single time the drawing surface got set up, the code assigns a freshly-built handle into a slot that already exists. Because of how C++ handles that exact combination (a destructor without matching move operations), the freshly-built temporary's destructor runs immediately afterward and releases the very same object the persistent slot just took ownership of. The surface gets deallocated inside its own setup function, before that function even returns - and every draw call after that reads freed memory.

This explains why the crash sometimes looked like a plain crash and sometimes said "unrecognized selector" - it depends entirely on what happens to reuse that freed memory first, not two different bugs. It also explains why v1.7's view-retain fix and v1.8's drop-MTKView fix both failed at the identical crash site: neither touched the actual bug, which was never in Swift/SwiftUI at all.

This is very likely a bug that's always existed, invisible on desktop (where this only runs once at startup, so the leftover dangling pointer can sit untouched for a whole session) - not something introduced by...

Fixes the recurring crash (BeginFrame -> nextDrawable) that survived the v1.7 fix. This is a real, structural fix, not another guess - but I want to be upfront: I'm not calling this "the last one" until it's actually confirmed.

## What was actually wrong

v1.7's fix (retaining the render surface's view) was real and necessary, but it wasn't the whole story - the crash kept recurring at the exact same spot afterward. The surface being used was an MTKView, which comes with its own built-in Metal rendering loop running 60 times a second - a leftover Swift-side placeholder from before the real C++ engine renderer existed. The real renderer's actual drawing surface was being added as a sublayer underneath that already-active, competing render loop: two independent Metal renderers fighting over the same piece of screen, one driven by the main thread, one by the game engine's own thread. That's exactly the kind of setup that produces intermittent, hard-to-pin-down crashes right at the drawable-request step - explaining why the crash location stayed identical even after the first, real fix.

## Fix

Dropped MTKView for this surface entirely and use a plain, ordinary view instead - one with no rendering machinery of its own, so the real engine has that screen space uncontested rather than sharing it with a leftover placeholder that was never actually connected to real game frames anyway.

Fixes the SIGSEGV you hit testing v1.6 - and this time the fix has strong independent confirmation, not just my own guess.

## What happened on v1.6

Real progress: the depth24Stencil8 fix from v1.6 worked completely - no more of that exception at all. Boot completed cleanly and the GPU thread actually started drawing frames. It then crashed with a genuine SIGSEGV inside MetalRenderer::BeginFrame() -> AcquireDrawable() -> nextDrawable().

LiveContainer's own crash reporter gave a more precise picture than our own log:

  -[OS_dispatch_data nextDrawable]: unrecognized selector sent to instance

That's the exact signature of a use-after-free: the object our code was calling nextDrawable on wasn't a CAMetalLayer anymore - the memory it used to occupy had been freed and reused by something completely unrelated (a GCD dispatch_data object), and our code was still holding the old, now-meaningless pointer.

## Root cause

The real CAMetalLayer is added as a sublayer of the SwiftUI-managed MTKView's own layer - and the C++ side holds a bare, unmanaged pointer to that sublayer with no memory-management awareness of its own. The Swift code handed that view to the C++ side without retaining it, meaning SwiftUI was free to tear down and recreate the view during the loading-screen transition - and when it did, the view's layer (and our sublayer) went with it, right out from under the GPU thread mid-use.

## Fix

Retain that view for the app's lifetime instead of letting SwiftUI manage it ...

This build fixes the exact crash you hit testing v1.5 - and unlike every previous fix tonight, this one comes with real confidence behind it, not a guess.

## What happened on v1.5

Real progress: boot completed end to end, no crash, no hang - the game screen actually appeared with buttons. That's M2's real finish line. The renderer still failed to construct, but survivably this time (the exception-safety fix from earlier caught it and logged the real reason instead of crashing):

  MetalRenderer construction/InitializeLayer threw: NSInvalidArgumentException
  - -[AGXA12XDevice isDepth24Stencil8PixelFormatSupported]: unrecognized
  selector sent to instance

## What that actually was

Not a mystery this time - a real, verifiable fact about the platform. `depth24Stencil8PixelFormatSupported` is a genuine, documented MTLDevice method, but Apple deliberately excludes it from the Metal API on iOS entirely. The legacy 24-bit-depth-plus-8-bit-stencil packed format isn't relevant to Apple Silicon GPUs (which use 32-bit-depth formats instead - already correctly handled elsewhere in this codebase regardless of this flag). Calling that method was always going to throw on every iOS device, every time - nothing specific to your hardware.

Guarded it, defaulted to false on iOS (the objectively correct answer), and it was the only call to that method anywhere in the code.

## What the crash actually was

Pulled the v1.4 dSYM and symbolicated the exact crash address (not a guess): it resolves precisely to `MetalRenderer::MetalRenderer()` - the C++ Metal renderer's constructor. The backtrace (objc_exception_throw, CoreFoundation message-forwarding frames) confirms this was a genuine, uncaught Objective-C/Metal exception - not a null-pointer bug. This constructor does real work that had never been exercised this early in the boot sequence before: Metal device/queue/texture creation, and compiling a Metal shader from source text at runtime.

## The fix

M2's actual goal is the interpreter/OS-HLE stack booting cleanly - not working rendering (that's the separate M3 milestone, still in progress). A renderer construction failure should never be able to crash the whole app over that. Wrapped both places that construct the renderer in `@try/@catch` (only possible in the Objective-C++ bridge file, not the plain C++ renderer code - Objective-C and C++ exceptions share one unwinding mechanism on Darwin, so this still catches it). Fixes the exact freeze you just hit testing v1.3 - stuck on the "Booting..." screen with zero log progress, not even the earliest boot checkpoint. That absence was the clue: it meant boot() was never even being called, not that it hung inside the C++ engine.

## Root cause of the v1.3 freeze

`MetalViewIOS` (the Metal-backed view that registers the render surface with the C++ bridge) sits in a plain SwiftUI VStack with no explicit `.frame(maxWidth:.infinity, maxHeight:.infinity)`. The registration code was waiting for that view's own `.bounds` to become nonzero before registering - a SwiftUI/UIKit layout-timing dependency that apparently never resolved. No crash, no log, no progress: indistinguishable from a real engine hang from the outside, but it was a Swift-side wiring gap, not a C++ bug.

**Fix:** register the surface immediately from `makeUIView()`, using `UIScreen.main.bounds` (always available, never zero) instead of waiting on the view's own layout. Exact pixel size only matters once M3 (real rendering) is further along; right now the GPU thread just needs a non-null surface to exist before it starts.

First build that actually links and runs since v1.2 testing surfaced a real boot freeze. Supersedes v1.2 - test this one, not that one.

## What's in this build

**Boot-freeze fixes** (from tonight's "press play, nothing happens, just freezes" investigation):
- `PPCTimer_init()` was never called anywhere in the iOS bridge - only desktop's `main.cpp` calls it. Without it, `LaunchForegroundTitle()`'s `PPCTimer_waitForInit()` spun forever on the main thread the instant boot() was called. Checkpoint logs confirmed this precisely: they stopped right after "about to call engine.boot()" and never reached "returned".
- `g_renderer` was never constructed before boot - only `cemu_bridge_register_render_surface()` did that, and nothing in the Swift app called it yet. The newly-spawned GPU thread calling `g_renderer->Initialize()` on a null pointer was a second freeze/crash risk chronologically *before* the PPCTimer fix even mattered.

**This should fix the launch crash.** Root cause found via the crash logger from the last release, confirmed by an actual on-device SIGABRT backtrace:

Three global JIT-context objects in \`BackendAArch64.cpp\` (the ARM64 recompiler backend) were declared at file scope, so C++ constructed them during static initialization - at binary load time, before \`main()\`, before Swift/SwiftUI ever ran. Each one's constructor eagerly allocated **executable JIT memory** via \`Xbyak_aarch64::MmapAllocator::alloc()\` (an \`mmap(PROT_EXEC)\` call). On iOS that needs a JIT/dynamic-codesigning entitlement a sideloaded app doesn't reliably have yet at pure launch - LiveContainer's JIT-enabling is a separate, slower, out-of-process step. The failed mmap threw an uncaught C++ exception with nothing to catch it (impossible at global-constructor scope), so the process \`abort()\`'d on every single launch.

Fix: converted all three to function-local statics, so construction is now lazy - deferred to first actual JIT use, which only happens well after the app has fully launched.

3. Whether it crashes or not, check `Documents/CemuCrashLog.txt` via Finder (Files tab) - if it crashes again, that file tells us whether the crash happens before or after Swift's own app lifecycle starts.

`Cemu.app.dSYM.zip` is included to symbolicate any real iOS crash report (e.g. via Console.app) alongside the checkpoint log.

Latest build - use this one. Includes everything so far:

**1. The original launch crash, fixed** - a global JIT-context object was
allocating executable memory at C++ static-init time (before main()), which
iOS doesn't allow that early for a sideloaded app. Fixed by deferring
construction to first actual use.

**2. The boot crash, fixed** - the same underlying JIT-memory-allocation
problem resurfaced the first time a title was actually booted (tapping the
game). Fixed by forcing interpreter mode - M2's exit test is about the
interpreter/OS-HLE stack, not JIT performance, so this sidesteps the open
question of whether genuine JIT memory allocation is even possible for a
sideloaded iOS app at all.

**3. A 20-agent audit, then fixes applied for what's real and relevant:**
- A second sibling of the exact static-init bug (CPU-feature-detection
  code that could also crash on some device/OS combos)
- A global background thread that was also spawning at static-init time
- Save games were completely non-functional (a required mount call was
  missing on the only launch path iOS uses)
- Per-title settings (CPU mode, audio, shaders) were leaking between titles
- Most plain log() calls throughout the whole engine were being silently
  dropped on iOS - meaning log.txt may have been incomplete every time it
  was checked this session
- An iOS-unavailable Metal API call in the renderer (relevant to upcoming
  M3 work)
- Two bugs in the new crash-logging code itself
- Two Swift crash risks...
